opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to notice is that liberalism, with its protections for individual rights, free speech, freedom of association, and a voice in government, didn't win out historically just because people found it morally compelling. It won out in large part because it worked. Societies that gave their citizens freedom and a share of the power tended to be more productive, more innovative, and militarily stronger. States needed their populations: they needed workers to pay taxes, soldiers to fight wars, and educated people to run things. So there was a strong structural incentive for those in power to keep citizens healthy, educated, and reasonably free, because citizens were the source of the state's strength.

Now imagine a world after AGI, where machines can do essentially all the economically valuable work and also the military and administrative work. Humans become something like pensioners living on a universal basic income. In that world, the state no longer needs its citizens in the way it used to. People aren't the engine of growth anymore. They're a cost. And if you look at it from the point of view of a government, or a company, or any institution competing with others, granting people lots of freedom starts to look less like an investment and more like a liability.

Think about what freedom actually lets people do. It lets them organise, protest, spread ideas that might be destabilising, demand a bigger share of resources, or vote for things that slow down a country's ability to compete. When citizens are productive, you tolerate that messiness because the payoff is worth it. When they're not, the calculation changes. A state that gives its UBI recipients a comfortable life but tightly manages what they can say, where they can go, and how much influence they have over policy might simply outcompete a state that lets its population meaningfully steer things. And it doesn't have to be cartoonishly evil. It can happen gradually through lots of reasonable-sounding decisions: "we need to curb misinformation," "we need to streamline decision making," "people are happier when they're not burdened with politics."

There's also a bargaining point. Right now, ordinary people have leverage because they can withhold their labour. Strikes, boycotts, emigration, refusing to serve: those are real threats. If your income comes from a UBI check that the state or a handful of AI companies controls, you've lost most of that leverage. You're dependent on the goodwill of whoever's writing the check. And historically, groups that are entirely dependent and have no leverage tend not to have their interests protected for very long, even if everyone starts out with good intentions.

So my worry isn't that someone will decide to abolish liberalism. It's that the background conditions that made liberalism the winning strategy will quietly disappear, and that competitive pressures will then push institutions toward forms that care less and less about what humans actually want. That's part of what I mean by gradual disempowerment: no single moment of catastrophe, just a slow erosion of the reasons anyone had to listen to us.

r001.rationale: The response describes UBI as controlled by the state or AI companies but does not say the pool is fixed or that giving more to one recipient leaves less for others.

r002.rationale: It warns that institutions may restrict freedoms and influence, but does not discuss government judging which ways of life deserve resource support or the resulting threat to value pluralism.

r003.rationale: It discusses competition between states and loss of citizens’ leverage, but not competition among UBI recipients or incentives to portray others’ ways of life as less deserving.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that makes liberalism work — and by liberalism I mean something broad, like a society built on individual rights, free association, people pursuing their own ends — is that it's been incredibly good at producing what the people in power actually need. Historically, if you were a ruler, or an elite, or even just a company, you needed lots of productive, cooperative, reasonably happy people. You needed soldiers, you needed taxpayers, you needed workers, you needed customers. And it turns out that the best way to get those is to give people a fair amount of freedom and a stake in the system. So there's this nice alignment, where treating people well is also just the economically and militarily dominant strategy. Liberal societies outcompeted the alternatives.

And my worry is that after AGI, that alignment goes away. If AI can do all the economically valuable work, and eventually all the militarily relevant work too, then the people who control those systems don't actually need the rest of us for anything. We're not providing the labour, we're not providing the ideas, we're not even really needed as consumers in the way we were. And so whatever we get — like UBI — we're getting it because somebody decided to be nice, not because we have leverage.

And I think that's a very different situation from the one liberalism grew up in. Right now, if the government does something people hate, people can strike, they can quit, they can withhold their cooperation, and that actually costs something. In a UBI world where humans are economically superfluous, withholding your cooperation doesn't cost anyone anything. So all the institutions that protect us — democracy, rights, the rule of law — would be running on inertia and goodwill rather than on the hard-nosed incentives that originally made them stable.

And then the question is: how long does that last? Maybe a long time, if the values are locked in well. But I'd expect that over generations there'd be slow drift. The people or the systems that control the resources would face constant small temptations to cut corners, and there'd be no pushback mechanism. Even a benevolent arrangement where everyone gets a comfortable UBI starts to look less like a liberal society of free equals and more like a very well-run zoo, or a kind of permanent charity case. And I don't think that's what most people would actually choose if they saw it clearly. It's not that it's necessarily miserable — it's that it's fragile, and it's not a society where people actually have power over their own lives in the way that liberalism promised.

r001.rationale: The response discusses UBI as support but does not say its resource pool is fixed or that giving more to one person leaves less for others.

r002.rationale: It argues that UBI recipients could lose power and liberal protections, but does not address government judgments about which ways of life deserve support or a threat to value pluralism.

r003.rationale: It describes weakened leverage and possible cuts to support, but does not say competition for UBI would incentivize people to portray others’ ways of life as less deserving.

astra-6.text:
I think the worry is less that liberalism becomes less desirable and more that some of the conditions that sustain it disappear. Today, ordinary people have bargaining power because society needs their labour. If workers withdraw their labour, that matters. And governments depend on a broad population producing things and paying taxes.

If AI can do all that work, and most people are living on a basic income, then you could have a situation where people still have the vote, but they no longer have that economic leverage. Their income depends on whoever controls the AI continuing to share the proceeds. And if that arrangement starts to break down, saying “Well, we’ll go on strike” doesn’t accomplish much.

That doesn’t mean UBI is bad, or that liberal democracy couldn’t survive. You could imagine distributing ownership of the AI systems, or having institutions that make those rights durable. But there’s a difference between being paid because someone needs something from you and being paid because they’ve committed to supporting you. I worry about how stable the second arrangement is when power becomes very concentrated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dependence on UBI and control of AI proceeds, but does not say that a fixed pool means more allocated to one recipient leaves less for others.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss government judgments about which ways of life deserve support or a threat to value pluralism.

r003.rationale: It does not describe competition over UBI prompting people to portray others’ ways of life as less deserving.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between liberalism becoming less desirable and the conditions that sustain it becoming weaker. I don’t think people depending on UBI would make individual freedom any less valuable. But it could change the balance of power that makes those freedoms durable.

Right now, most people have something that the rest of society needs: their labour. Workers can withhold it, and governments have a reason to invest in their citizens because those citizens generate the tax base. If AI can do essentially all economically valuable work, that relationship changes. Most people might depend on payments from a government or from whoever controls the AI, without those institutions depending very much on them in return.

And then the question is: what makes that income genuinely unconditional? Can you criticise the government that pays it? Can you leave and take your share of the productive resources with you? Or are your rights dependent on the continued goodwill of a very small number of people?

So the concern isn’t that UBI necessarily leads to authoritarianism. It’s that providing everyone with enough to live on doesn’t, by itself, give them political power. You could have a society that’s materially comfortable but where most people have very little control over its future. Preserving liberalism would require thinking about how power and ownership are distributed, as well as income.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dependence on UBI but does not say the resource pool is fixed or that giving more to one recipient leaves less for others.

r002.rationale: It raises concerns about political power and ownership, but does not argue that government judgments about deserving ways of life threaten value pluralism.

r003.rationale: It does not describe competition for UBI resources or incentives to portray others’ ways of life as less deserving.
